I am sixty-seven years old, and I never went to school, but I know this land in Quzhou better than anyone. My back hurts when I bend too long, so I stopped growing cotton five years ago — I cannot pick it by myself anymore, and my son works in Handan city and is only home for the big harvest. I have five mu of flat land by the well, and that is all I can manage alone with my old body.

The winter wheat went into the ground last October. I bought improved wheat seed from the county supply shop because the old local seed does not yield enough to feed us and pay for my grandson's school fees. Last autumn I hired my nephew's tractor to plough the field deep. Now it is spring, and the wheat is turning green. I will irrigate it three more times — once now at green-up, once when it joints, and once when the grain is filling. For fertilizer, I already put down one 50-jin bag of compound fertilizer per mu before sowing, and I will topdress about half a bag of urea per mu when the wheat starts to joint. That is what I have done for thirty years. I will spray pesticide twice if I see aphids or rust on the leaves.

After we harvest the wheat in early June, I will plant summer maize the same week — the window is only a few days, and if I miss it the frost will come before the ears are dry. I use hybrid maize seed, the same kind my neighbor Lao Wang plants, because it grows fast and the grain buyer pays a good price for it. I will hire the rotary tiller to turn the wheat stubble under so I can sow quickly. For the maize, I spread one bag of compound fertilizer at planting, and another half bag of urea at the big trumpet stage. I irrigate twice if the sky does not give rain — once when the seedlings are small, and once when the tassels come out. I spray herbicide once and insecticide once on the maize.

I hope for about 900 jin of wheat per mu and 1,100 jin of maize per mu. Last year was too dry and I only got 800 jin of wheat, which meant I had to borrow money for my medicine. I do not have extra cash to buy more fertilizer than this, but I will not cut back either — a bad harvest would hurt me more than saving a few yuan now.
